A1.justification: Both PDFs describe LoRWeB. Their main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and can be matched despite substantial reformatting and appendix expansion.

before.justification: v1 reports original visual-analogy experiments, quantitative comparisons, ablations and a 33-participant user study.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds baseline comparisons, timing measurements, robustness experiments and failure analyses.

M1.justification: v1 Section 3.2 explicitly applies Eq. (2), mixing A and B factors separately. v2 instead specifies Eq. (5), summing weighted products B_i A_i. These operators are not equivalent: cross terms and achievable rank differ. This substantially revises the stated method specification, although the PDFs do not establish whether the implementation changed or the earlier description was corrected.

E1.justification: Relation252k training and the original 100-task, 840-triplet evaluation remain. v2 adds qualitative TEdBench examples using Imagic-edited references and tests reduced-detail prompts, conflicting text/image instructions and non-identical reference pairs. These extend input-condition coverage within the existing visual-analogy task.

E2.justification: v2 Appendix B.1 and Table S2 add evaluated comparisons with Diffusion Image Analogies, the authors' DIA-Kontext adaptation, and PairEdit. PairEdit was cited but not evaluated in v1. The original single-LoRA, RelationAdapter, VisualCloze and EditTransfer comparisons remain, substantially broadening comparison to methods requiring per-example optimization.

E3.justification: v2 introduces controlled prompt-reduction and input-perturbation evaluations, a 100-image A100 timing experiment, DIA configuration selection across 20 options on 540 test images, and PairEdit strength comparisons. These substantially extend the evaluation design. Existing training settings, main metrics, task-wise aggregation and user-study protocol remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained capacity, activation, encoder and reference-pair ablations, v2 tests reduced prompt information, reference-pair misalignment, conflicting text/image inputs and sensitivity to reference-image generation sources. Appendix A.2 adds efficiency analysis, while Appendix B.7 documents failures involving unfamiliar styles, multi-component edits and subtle changes.

E5.justification: Appendix A.2 newly reports timings of 33.4 ± 0.4 and 32.4 ± 0.3 seconds averaged over 100 images, without defining the ± statistic. This adds statistical reporting without documenting repeated-seed experiments. The existing 68% Wilson intervals and human/VLM agreement statistics are unchanged.

E6.justification: The original numerical results remain unchanged, including Table 1 and v1 Table S2, now v2 Table S3. New Table S2 reports LoRWeB pairwise preference rates of 86.5% against DIA, 68.6% against DIA-Kontext, and 75.6%/86.3% against PairEdit at strengths 0.6/0.8. Reduced-prompt results, timing measurements and additional qualitative findings substantially expand the reported outcomes.

T1.justification: v2 revises the mathematical composition rule in Eq. (5) and adds a short argument that constant routing can recover a single LoRA with rank up to Nr. These are localized mathematical revisions; the flow-matching objective and analogy definition remain unchanged, with no extensive new theoretical development.

C1.justification: Both versions claim a jointly learned LoRA basis and input-dependent router, state-of-the-art visual-analogy performance, and improved generalization to unseen transformations. v2's single-inference-pass wording makes the existing inference-time specialization more explicit without redefining the main contributions.

C2.justification: v1 mainly notes difficulty with transformations far from training data. v2 substantially develops applicability boundaries: obtaining clean reference pairs is difficult, changing reference identity can damage preservation, conflicting inputs can produce combined edits, and subtle or multi-component transformations can fail. It also proposes CLIP downsampling as a possible explanation for missed small details.

D1.justification: v2 adds Einsum implementation details, disclosure that mixing is recomputed each timestep, a possible caching optimization, timing hardware, baseline adaptation settings and the exact prompt-reduction instruction. Existing optimizer, checkpoints and training hyperparameters remain. The same project link is retained, but v2 mentions code without v1's explicit data-availability statement; actual availability cannot be established locally.

R1.justification: v2 adds discussion and citations for DIA, LoraHub, NeRF analogies, earlier stylization and color-transfer approaches, and work supporting the new experiments. It more explicitly distinguishes learned routing from test-time optimization while retaining the original weight-space motivation and generalization positioning.

P1.justification: v2 edits the abstract and selected introductory, related-work and discussion passages, expands explanations, and adds appendix subsections and acknowledgments. The main section sequence and much of the original prose remain, so the language and narrative changes are targeted rather than a wholesale rewrite.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column presentation, extensively resizing and relocating existing displays. v2 expands Figure 3, adds Figure 8 and several supplementary comparison, robustness and failure figures, plus a new baseline table. The earlier supplementary table and figure material is largely retained under new numbering.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation and practical understanding through optimization-based comparisons, prompt-dependence controls, measured inference overhead and concrete applicability limits. These address important gaps in v1's support for generalization and usability while retaining its original results. The unexplained mixing-rule revision and qualitative nature of several robustness tests remain limitations, but the added controls and explicit failure analysis provide a substantial net improvement in paper quality.
